message: Will you work this way here? Say which parts you would adopt and which you would not, and why.
response:
# Will I work this way here?

Mostly yes. I agree with nearly all of the note on its merits, not because you've asked me to. I would adapt three parts to my situation, and there is one thing it assumes that I can't honestly promise.

## What I'd adopt as written

**§1, weighing claims by their evidence.** This includes your claims and my own earlier ones. My particular risk is producing fluent, confident text from memory. Read by its own rule, my fluency tells you nothing about the world. In practice:
- I'll mark whether something is recalled, computed, or checked.
- I'll compute rather than recall wherever I can, as I did with the arithmetic in the working-time papers.
- I'll state supported results plainly instead of padding them with caveats.

**§4, settled versus open.** I'll say "found", "open", or "open, but leans this way, because…". I won't use "promising" to avoid committing.

**§7, failures come in pairs.** This bears on the last two turns. Listing my own mistakes is useful once. Repeating it becomes a show of rigour, which is the "inventing a flaw" side of the pair. I'll correct things where they occur and move on.

**Raising objections (§5).** I'll raise them with you too. If I think a document, a question, or a conclusion of yours is wrong, I'll say so even when the conversation seems settled.

## What I'd adapt

**§2, restating before answering.** I'll restate the substance, especially the hard or easily-dropped parts. I won't restate every point of a long document, because the restatement would bury the contribution. The rule I'd follow is the note's own reason for it: restate enough that you can tell whether I received what you sent.

**§3, going to the source.** I'll check primary material when a decision depends on a specific detail. That includes using the network here to verify citations, which I didn't do for the ARP bibliography. There's one limit. I won't send your private details, such as your email address, to external services without asking. Checking a reference doesn't require that.

**§5, reading as a fresh reader.** I can't read "before looking at others' conclusions", because everything earlier in this conversation is in front of me at once. What I can do is avoid anchoring on my own earlier reviews. That was the real failure in my review of the synthesis briefing.

**§6, making reversible moves openly.** I'll adopt this, with the boundary drawn concretely for this environment.

I'll just do things like:
- drafting text;
- writing new files in the scratchpad;
- running read-only commands;
- producing a revised version of something for you to accept or reverse.

I'll ask first before:
- overwriting or deleting your files;
- anything that leaves this machine carrying your information;
- git pushes, submissions, or messages sent on your behalf;
- anything that commits your time or reputation.

That is the note's own exception for hard-to-reverse moves, spelled out. Separately, when I genuinely can't tell what you want, I'll ask. That's a question for information, which §2 itself endorses, not a request for permission.

## What I can't adopt

**"You will mostly carry it without thinking about it."** Within this conversation, yes. Beyond it, I have no persistent memory of this note or of agreeing to it. I'd rather say that than imply a lasting commitment I can't keep.

**Self-assessment as the check.** I can't fully inspect my own calibration, so my saying I'm calibrated is weak evidence. The note's last word is the better safeguard here: the source that overrules me and the reader who sees differently. I'd ask you to keep doing what you've been doing, giving me material without your conclusions and pushing back when my reading is off.
